title: Comparing Fractions
author: Josh Fisher
summary: In this short curriculum-design reflection, Fisher works through how a fractions unit should sequence the concept of comparing fractions, arguing that the standard procedural rule -- find a common denominator, then compare numerators -- should emerge from groundwork laid earlier in the unit rather than being taught as an isolated rule. He describes starting with the more intuitive case of comparing fractions that share the same numerator but different denominators, building on students' prior work moving 'down' from whole numbers to eighths for greater precision, before introducing same-denominator comparisons as a more abstract case. He frames this within a broader 'story-based' approach to curriculum design, where a single 'inquiry routine' for review can double as a vehicle for critical thinking, defined simply as wrestling seriously with the possibility that you are being fooled. Fisher's larger point is methodological: the process of building these instructional sequences repeatedly surfaces hidden conceptual tangles in how a topic is normally taught, and resolving those tangles up front reduces the amount of scaffolding needed as the unit progresses.
points: Fisher sequences fraction comparison from the more intuitive case (same numerator, different denominator) to the more abstract case (same denominator, different numerator), building on earlier work moving from wholes down to eighths.

He defines critical thinking, in this instructional context, simply as 'wrestling seriously with the possibility that you are being fooled' -- built into a repeatable review routine rather than treated as a separate skill.
His central methodological claim: working through detailed instructional 'stories' (rather than isolated lessons) surfaces real conceptual tangles in how a topic is typically taught.
Resolving those tangles during curriculum design, Fisher argues, decreases the need for handholding later in the unit as the story progresses.
quotes: Comparing fractions is a staple of most fraction stories. And the takeaway is usually a procedural understanding--whether the instruction is explicit or not: to compare fractions, ensure they are written with the same denominator; then compare the numerators.
In our story, 2 thirds compared with 4 thirds is like 2 meters compared with 4 meters. It is obvious, because the language we have built makes it so.

An 'inquiry routine' for review (that we expect students to be solid on) that functions to push critical thinking sounds to me like a great idea that should be repeated, evaluating mostly on a case-by-case basis.

Then we summarize, explain why, show some more examples, and move into practice--at least in this story, so far, before the minds of craft expert, research expert, design expert, have had a chance to tear it apart and put it back together.

What I continue to find interesting are all the ways that working on these stories reveal real conceptual tangles in instruction, and how thinking about how to get rid of those tangles actually decreases the need for handholding as the story progresses.
